tagline: Prayer times, the Qibla and the Qur'an, without ads or tracking.

home.headline: Turn your face to the Qibla
home.sentence: An iPhone app for prayer times, the Qibla and the whole Qur'an. Free, without ads, and nothing about you is collected.

times.heading: Times as your mosque keeps them
times.text: Wajh calculates the prayers the way the mosques in your country do, also when you travel, and follows Diyanet when the app is in Turkish. Each time can move a few minutes to match your mosque exactly, and the night shows its middle and its last third.

quran.heading: The mushaf, page by page
quran.text: All 604 pages of the Madinah mushaf, turned like paper. Ten reciters read verse by verse while the page follows them, also with the screen locked, and any part can be downloaded to listen offline.

private.heading: Nothing about you is collected
private.text: No account, no ads and no tracking. Your settings, tasbih and tracker stay on your iPhone. Place names and the map come from Apple Maps, the recitations from the app's own audio server, and Makkah live from YouTube.

items.a: Yes, all of it: no ads, no subscription, nothing to buy.
Any iPhone with iOS 18 or later.
The times, the Qibla and the text of the Qur'an all work offline. A recitation needs internet, unless you downloaded it first.

close.text: As in the verse “So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque” (al-Baqarah 2:144). Free on the App Store, for iPhone.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: Wajh (called “Qibla & Prayer” on the Home Screen) is made by Melih Sivrikaya. This policy explains what happens to your data when you use the app.
privacy.summary: In short: I don't collect data about you. There is no account, no advertising, no analytics code and no tracking. To name your place, search for a city and show the map and mosques nearby, your iPhone asks Apple Maps. To play a recitation of the Qur'an, it downloads the audio from the app's own audio server, where I keep no record of who listens; Makkah live plays a stream from YouTube. See below.

sections.heading: Who is responsible
paragraphs: I, Melih Sivrikaya (support@qibla.dev), am responsible for this app and for the personal data described in this policy (the “controller” under the GDPR). Apple is responsible for its own services that the app uses: Apple Maps, Siri, crash reporting and iCloud Backup. Cloudflare runs the app's audio server for me, as my processor, and Google is responsible for YouTube.

The app asks Apple Maps and the audio server only for what the features you use need. I run the audio server, answer emails and use the reports Apple passes on because of my legitimate interest in offering, supporting and improving the app (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR).

sections.heading: Your location
paragraphs: The app uses your iPhone's location to calculate prayer times and the direction of the Qibla, to suggest the calculation method used in your country, and to let the compass use true north. That calculation happens on your iPhone.

Some features use Apple Maps, so Apple receives what they need: your location, when the app looks up the name, country and time zone of your place (when it starts, and again after you have moved more than about a kilometre); what you type in the city search, as you type it; and, when you open the Qibla map, the area around you or around the city you chose, to show the map and search it for mosques. Tapping a mosque opens it in the Apple Maps app. The app adds nothing that identifies you. Apple handles these requests under its own privacy policy (apple.com/legal/privacy).

The app asks for your location only while you use it (“While Using the App”), so iOS never gives it your location in the background. It saves the last place it found; Siri's answers and the reminders it schedules in the background use that saved place. You can also use the app without location access: choose a city, and turn location access off for the app in your iPhone's Settings.

sections.heading: What stays on your iPhone
paragraphs: The app stores your settings (including your school and calculation method), the last place it found or the city you chose (name and coordinates), the tasbih count, the tracker (the days you marked as fasting, the fasts to make up and the missed prayers), and your reading progress in the Qur'an. They are kept on your iPhone, not on any server, and are not synced through iCloud. Like other app data, they are included in your iPhone's backups (iCloud Backup or a backup on your computer), if you make them. Deleting the app removes them from your iPhone.
Reminders are scheduled on your iPhone itself; no server sends them. The iftar countdown and the next prayer on the Lock Screen also run on your iPhone.

sections.heading: Recitations of the Qur'an
paragraphs: When you play a recitation in the Qur'an tab, your iPhone downloads the audio of each verse from the app's own audio server (audio.qibla.dev) and keeps it, so that no verse is downloaded twice; iOS may remove these files when it needs space. Like any website, the server receives your IP address and which verse and reciter your iPhone asks for; the app sends nothing else. The server runs on Cloudflare, which handles these requests for me under its data processing terms. I keep no record of who listens. A surah, juz or the whole Qur'an you download to listen offline stays on your iPhone until you remove it in the app.

sections.heading: The camera
paragraphs: The Qibla camera shows the camera's live picture with the direction of Mecca on it. The picture stays on your iPhone: nothing is recorded, saved or sent. The app asks for camera access only when you open it.

sections.heading: Makkah live
paragraphs: When you open Makkah live in the Qibla tab, the app asks this website (qibla.dev) which stream is on, then shows YouTube's own player with the live stream of the Saudi Quran TV channel, in YouTube's privacy-enhanced mode (youtube-nocookie.com). YouTube (Google) then receives your IP address and what its player needs, and may store its own cookies, under Google's privacy policy (policies.google.com/privacy). The app sends YouTube nothing else.

sections.heading: Siri and Shortcuts
paragraphs: When you ask Siri for a prayer time, Apple handles your question as it does for any app. The app works out the answer on your iPhone, without opening, from the settings and the place saved there.

sections.heading: Crash reports and statistics
paragraphs: If you share analytics with app developers (in your iPhone's Settings: Privacy & Security, Analytics & Improvements), Apple sends me crash reports and statistics about how the app performs and is used, such as the number of sessions. Apple also shows me totals such as the number of downloads per country. Apple collects this itself, under its own privacy policy, and says it does not identify you; the app contains no code for it. I use it only to fix problems and improve the app.

sections.heading: No advertising or tracking
paragraphs: The app contains no advertising, analytics or tracking code. Besides Apple's own frameworks it uses only Adhan, an open-source library that calculates prayer times on your iPhone and sends nothing anywhere. Apart from the requests described above, the app shares nothing with anyone. I don't collect personal data from anyone, including children.

sections.heading: If you email me
paragraphs: If you email me, I receive your email address, your name if you give it, and what you write. I use them only to answer you, and I delete the conversation once it is no longer needed, or sooner if you ask. My email provider stores the emails for me.

sections.heading: Your rights
paragraphs: Apart from emails you send me, I keep no personal data about you. For those emails you can ask me for a copy, ask me to correct or delete them, ask me to limit how I use them, or object to how I use them. Everything the app stores is on your iPhone: you can change it in the app, or remove all of it by deleting the app. Data held by Apple is handled by Apple (apple.com/legal/privacy).
If you think I handle your data wrongly, you can complain to a data protection authority, for example the one in the country where you live.

sections.heading: Changes
paragraphs: If this policy changes, the new version will appear on this page with a new date.

support.title: Support
support.intro: A question, a problem, or a time that doesn't match your mosque? Email support@qibla.dev.

faq.q: The times differ from my mosque's timetable.
faq.a: Mosques use different calculation methods, mostly for Fajr and Isha. In Settings, choose the method your mosque uses: each one shows today's Fajr and Isha, so you can compare them with your mosque's timetable. Check the Asr setting too, and if a time is still a few minutes off, move it under Adjust times.

faq.q: The Hijri date is a day off.
faq.a: The app follows the Umm al-Qura calendar, or Diyanet's calendar when you use the Diyanet method. Where you live, the month can start a day earlier or later because of moon sighting. You can move the Hijri date by a day or two in Settings.

faq.q: The compass points the wrong way.
faq.a: Hold your iPhone flat, away from metal, magnets and other electronics, and move it in a figure eight to calibrate the compass. Allow location access, so the compass can use true north instead of magnetic north.

Check that notifications are allowed for the app in your iPhone's Settings, that the bell next to the prayer is on, and that no Focus mode is holding them back. Open the app now and then: iOS keeps a limited number of reminders waiting. The app schedules the next days each time you open it, and now and then in the background if Background App Refresh is on for it.

faq.q: The iftar countdown doesn't appear on my Lock Screen.
faq.a: Start it yourself: from the Ramadan card on the Prayer times tab, or in the Tracker after turning on “I'm fasting today”. It can start from 8 hours before iftar, and Live Activities must be allowed for the app in your iPhone's Settings.

faq.q: Does the app collect my data?
faq.a: No. Nothing about you is collected. Place names, city search and the map use Apple Maps, and recitations come from the app's own audio server, where I keep no record of who listens; the privacy policy has the details.

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.intro: “Qibla & Prayer” should work for everyone. This page says what the app does for accessibility today, and how to tell me when something doesn’t work for you.

sections.heading: What the app supports
paragraphs: VoiceOver: every button, icon and control has a spoken label, and the Qibla screen tells you which way to turn. The Qur’an is read with an Arabic voice, and each verse on a page is an action (in the rotor) that opens it to copy, share or play.
Voice Control: every control has a name you can say, matching what you see. Say “Show actions” on a Qur’an page to open one of its verses.

Larger Text: text grows with the text size set on your iPhone, up to the largest accessibility sizes. At those sizes the monthly timetable lists each day’s times instead of seven columns. The Qur’an page also has its own text size in its menu. The tasbih’s count grows until it fills its circle.
Dark interface: the app is dark, with light text, and so is the Qur’an. For a light paper page, choose Paper in its settings.
Contrast: all text has a contrast of at least 6.3 to 1 against its background. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) ask for 4.5 to 1.

Not by colour alone: the next prayer and the next day in the Islamic calendar have a diamond in front, today’s row in the tables is bold, and a selected choice has a check mark. A bell that is off is crossed out. In the Qur’an, the verse being recited or found is highlighted, and also underlined when Differentiate Without Colour is on.
Reduce Motion: when it is on in your iPhone’s accessibility settings, the compass, the setup and the tasbih counter no longer animate, and the Qur'an's pages slide instead of curling.
Captions: when the Qur’an is recited, the page shows the Arabic text being recited and marks the verse. The recitation is the text on the page, with nothing added.
Haptics: your iPhone taps when you face the Qibla, with every count of the tasbih, and when a round is complete.
Languages: English, Dutch, German, French, Turkish and Arabic. Arabic reads right to left.

sections.heading: Good to know
paragraphs: Makkah live is YouTube's live stream from the Masjid al-Haram, in YouTube's own player: it has captions when YouTube provides them, and no audio descriptions. The app has no other video.

Every build runs Apple’s automated accessibility audit on each screen, at the normal and the largest text size. Such an audit can’t find everything, so please tell me if something doesn’t work for you.

sections.heading: This website
paragraphs: This website is plain HTML with headings and no scripts, and follows your browser’s text size and zoom.

sections.heading: Tell me what doesn’t work
paragraphs: If something in the app is hard to see, hear, reach or understand, please email support@qibla.dev. It helps to mention your iPhone model, your iOS version and the accessibility settings you use.
